strengths: The paper introduces a well-motivated extension of theory-based RL (TBRL) that addresses two acknowledged technical bottlenecks in prior work (e.g., EMPA): restrictive theory languages and slow planning. Replacing VGDL-based theory induction with LLM-synthesized Python world models is a sensible and interesting direction.

The bilevel planning architecture is clearly described and grounded in the PDDL/bilevel-planning literature; the integration of Fast Downward with low-level BFS using a learned Python transition model is coherent.

The empirical results across Sokoban, Push Boulders 1, BabyAI, and KekeCompetition show substantial gains (e.g., 24.5x reduction in API usage) and demonstrate real transferability of the learned world model from KekeCompetition to Baba is AI (all 40 levels solved without additional learning), which is a striking and non-trivial result.
The ablation on bilevel planning (Table 3) provides direct evidence that the hierarchical structure meaningfully reduces planning time, supporting one of the paper's central claims.
The paper is generally well-organized, connects to cognitive science motivation, and includes sample prompts in the appendix.
weaknesses: The most directly comparable prior methods (Tang et al. 2024 WorldCoder; Dainese et al. 2024 code world models; AutumnSynth) are discussed in related work but never used as baselines. The only comparison is to an LLM-only agent (GPT-o1), so it is unclear whether the specific bilevel + synthesized-world-model design is what drives performance versus the mere presence of any explicit model.

The comparison to GPT-o1 is potentially confounded. If the GPT-o1 baseline still fails when given the ground-truth transition model and the high-level plan ('heavy' prompting, Table 5), this suggests the baseline may be failing for prompt-interface or action-decoding reasons rather than for lack of a world model. The paper does not analyze why the heavily-prompted baseline fails, which undermines the central claim that explicit code world models are the source of improvement.

The API-call metric treats GPT-4o (TheoryCoder) and GPT-o1 (baseline) calls as equivalent, ignoring the very large cost/latency differences between these models. A cost-normalized or token-normalized comparison would be more honest and would likely reduce the reported '24.5x' advantage.

The abstract operators and predicates are hand-designed for each domain (acknowledged in the limitations), so the paper overstates the degree to which the agent 'learns' a theory; the transferred abstractions largely encode the solution structure (e.g., push_to_hole, boxes_stuck, move_between_bottleneck, form_rule/break_rule). The framework therefore inherits, rather than resolves, EMPA's hand-designed hypothesis-space problem.

Experimental scope is limited: a few levels per game (5, 4, 17, 13), deterministic grid-world domains only, and no information about the number of random seeds or variance for the API-call tables. Single-run numbers make it hard to assess reliability of reported gains, and the runtime table (e.g., Sokoban level 1: 24.58s vs TIMEOUT; the '-/-' cell for Push Boulders level 1) is underexplained and inconsistent (level 1 slower than level 3 for Bilevel).

No ablation isolating the LLM component (e.g., using a weaker LLM at both stages), no ablation of the number of random exploration steps (only 'up to 10 random actions'), and no analysis of how sensitive results are to the choice/model version of GPT-4o. Reproducibility is weakened by reliance on a specific closed-source LLM and the absence of a stated code/artifact release.

strengths: Integrates theory-based RL with LLM program synthesis and bilevel PDDL planning in a coherent, cognitively motivated architecture, and the high-level/low-level split is presented clearly (Figures 1–3).

The sample-efficiency gains over the LLM-only baseline are striking and consistent across domains (e.g., KekeCompetition 49 -> 2 API calls; BabyAI 49 -> 2; up to a reported 24.5x reduction), and the ablation in Table 3 shows large planning-time savings from abstractions.

The demonstration that a world model synthesized for KekeCompetition transfers to Baba is AI and solves levels without additional learning (Fig. 12, Sec. 4.6) is a genuinely interesting result about the compositionality of code-based models.
Labeling the replay buffer by grounded abstract operators to steer LLM refinement (Fig. 2, Fig. 9) is a sensible, reusable mechanism for grounding errors to high-level concepts.
The prompts are included in the appendix, which partially supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'general-purpose abstractions' is not supported: the PDDL domain files, problem files, predicates, and the checker that bridges abstract effects to low-level states are all hand-designed per domain (Sec. 3.3.1, Figs. 6–10). The paper itself concedes this ('hand engineering useful abstractions can be tedious', Limitations). What actually remains learned is only the low-level transition model, so the contribution is largely LLM-based transition synthesis plus off-the-shelf Fast Downward + BFS.

The baseline is weak and possibly unfair. GPT-o1 is prompted directly with a text state description and given feedback transitions, but no comparison is made to other world-model LLM agents (e.g., WorldCoder, Tang et al. 2024), neural model-based RL, or hierarchical RL. API-call counts are also highly sensitive to prompt design and the 'up to 5 retries' budget, and no statistical analysis or error bars are reported for any metric.

The empirical scope is small and the framing is inconsistent with it: only a handful of levels per domain (Sokoban 5, Push Boulders 4, BabyAI 17, Keke 13), with single-valued counts and no seeds. Although 'task success rate' is defined in Sec. 4.1 and repeatedly claimed ('higher success rates'), success-rate numbers are never actually reported; results are almost entirely API-call counts.

Question 4 ('Does it solve the subset of games EMPA failed on?') is never answered empirically — EMPA is not re-run and no head-to-head comparison is provided; the paper only asserts the advantage (Sec. 4.2, Conclusion).

There are concrete presentation/consistency errors that undermine confidence: table captions and data appear misaligned (Table 1/2/3 ordering versus the text's stated ordering), and the text states 'In Push Boulders 1, level 1 runtime is the same for Bilevel and Ablated' while the table shows 24.58s vs TIMEOUT. These are not cosmetic given they concern the headline runtime ablation.

The method's applicability is narrow: BFS low-level planning with deterministic, discrete, small-state models, and the authors acknowledge symbolic planning cost 'could grow' for larger domains (Sec. 4.5). Claims about generalizing 'beyond VGDL' via Python are under-exercised by the small grid-worlds used.

Reproducibility is incomplete: full PDDL domain/problem files, domain descriptions, and the exact BFS/Fast-Downward configurations are not provided, and no code release is mentioned, making independent reproduction difficult despite the prompt appendix.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work (EMPA, WorldCoder, Dainese et al., Wong et al.); the technical advances (LLM for approximate inference over the transition model; reuse of hand-coded PDDL abstractions; standard bilevel planning) are combinations of existing components rather than a new capability, and the paper does not isolate which component drives the reported gains.

strengths: Combines PDDL-based bilevel planning with LLM-synthesized Python transition models, a novel and well-motivated integration of TBRL, program synthesis, and hierarchical planning.

Demonstrates strong empirical gains: substantially fewer API calls than GPT-o1 across Sokoban, Push Boulders 1, BabyAI, and KekeCompetition; solves levels where LLM-only planning fails; shows zero-shot transfer from KekeCompetition to Baba is AI.
Ablation on bilevel planning shows large runtime improvements and avoidance of timeouts, supporting the benefit of abstract subplans for search efficiency.
The method is clearly described with algorithm, figures, and examples; limitations section is candid about hand-engineered abstractions and future work.
weaknesses: The high-level PDDL operators/predicates and problem/domain files are hand-crafted per domain, not learned. This is the core limitation: the claimed 'transferable knowledge' is given, so the method does not yet achieve the paper's broader TBRL goal of flexible transferable abstractions.

The main comparison against GPT-o1 does not isolate the contribution of the LLM-synthesized Python transition model from the hand-coded hierarchical abstractions and bilevel planner. Closest program-synthesis world-model baselines (e.g., WorldCoder, Dainese et al.) are not compared, so the claim of superiority over existing structured world-model approaches is not established.
Evaluation is limited to deterministic, discrete 2D grid worlds/levels; no stochastic, continuous, or more challenging complexity settings are tested, despite claims about extending beyond VGDL.

Sample efficiency is measured only by API calls, not environment interactions or wall-clock/token cost; no variance/error bars/seeds for API calls or success rates are reported, weakening statistical rigor.
Reproducibility is incomplete: no code/data release is mentioned; exact PDDL files, prompt traces, and LLM version outputs are not fully specified; API results may vary over time.
Some claims are overstated (e.g., 'approaches based on directly synthesizing a policy perform poorly') since no policy-synthesis baseline is evaluated.

strengths: The paper presents a technically coherent system, TheoryCoder, that combines LLM-based synthesis of a Python low-level transition model with PDDL high-level abstractions and bilevel planning; this directly targets two acknowledged limitations of prior TBRL work: restrictive VGDL theory language and poor planning scalability.

The experimental results provide evidence for substantial API-call sample efficiency over an LLM-only planner: e.g., Table 8 reports 1 vs. 25 API calls on Sokoban, 1 vs. 19 on Push Boulders 1, 2 vs. 49 on BabyAI, and 7 vs. 39 on KekeCompetition.

On VGDL domains where EMPA struggled, TheoryCoder succeeds on all tested levels with fewer environment steps in Sokoban and solves Push Boulders 1 levels that EMPA failed (Table 3); the comparison to WorldCoder on MiniGrid/BabyAI also reports higher success (100% vs. 83%) with fewer tokens.

The ablation in Table 4 supports the planning-efficiency claim: bilevel planning is much faster than an ablated low-level-only planner and a manually authored pure PDDL/Fast-Downward approach, with several timeouts in the ablations.
The paper discusses limitations and failure modes, including dependence on hand-engineered abstractions and a goop/sacrifice failure mode, and attempts a contamination check with a custom game.
weaknesses: The method's high-level abstractions are not learned: the PDDL operators, predicates, domain files, and problem files are manually designed per environment. The manuscript acknowledges this, but it means the central TBRL problem of acquiring transferable abstractions remains largely assumed rather than solved, and the generality claim is substantially constrained.

The comparisons are not prior-matched. TheoryCoder receives hand-designed domain-specific abstractions and descriptions, while the LLM-only baseline does not, making the strong sample-efficiency advantage less informative about the proposed learning mechanism. Similarly, the WorldCoder comparison does not control for the hand-provided PDDL structure.

Evaluation is limited to deterministic 2D grid-worlds and a small number of levels. There is little statistical rigor: success rates appear single-run, planning times average only 5 runs, no confidence intervals or seeds are reported, and robustness is discussed only qualitatively.

Sample efficiency is measured mainly by API calls and tokens rather than environment interactions or total planner/compute cost. BFS simulation, Fast Downward calls, and extensive low-level search are not fully reflected in the main efficiency comparisons, and the only environment-step comparison is confined to VGDL (Table 3).

Reproducibility is weak: no code or artifact release is mentioned, experiments rely on proprietary LLM APIs (GPT-4o/GPT-o1) and custom environments, and key details such as which levels are used, exact prompts, retry/planner budgets, and variance are not sufficiently standardized.

The custom-game contamination check reports only TheoryCoder API/token usage (Table 15), with no baseline or level results, so it does not convincingly establish that the main results are independent of training-data contamination.

Some claims are overbroad or speculative. The paper frames the work as human-inspired TBRL and suggests broad implications for cognitive science, but no human experiments or cognitive modeling evaluations are provided. Cross-domain transfer is not demonstrated; only within-domain reuse and a shared-mechanics Baba variant are shown.

strengths: The problem framing is well motivated: extending theory-based RL beyond VGDL with a more expressive (Python) theory language and more scalable planning is a sensible research direction, and the paper clearly situates itself relative to EMPA, WorldCoder, and bilevel planning/PDDL work.

The system is genuinely applied to a non-trivial domain (KekeCompetition/Baba is You) where rule formation/breaking and transmutation must be inferred, and it is shown to solve levels that a strong LLM-only planner (GPT-o1) fails.

The paper attempts several useful ablations: bilevel vs. non-bilevel planning runtimes, a purely PDDL Fast-Downward baseline, API-call budgets, a 'heavy' prompting condition for the LLM baseline, and a contamination check on a newly designed custom game.

The limitations section is honest about hand-engineering abstractions, overgeneralization failure modes (sacrifice levels in Baba is You), and the open question of how to learn abstractions themselves.
weaknesses: The central claim of fast grounding/generalization is undermined because the transferable knowledge is not learned or transferred automatically: the PDDL domain files (operators/predicates) and, importantly, the PDDL problem files (goals and initial abstract state) are hand-designed per game and, in some cases, per level. The paper concedes this, but it means most of what makes the agent succeed is provided by the human designer, not learned, making the headline claims (sample efficiency, generalization to new domains) much weaker than presented.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor. Success rates and API-call counts appear to be single runs despite temperature=0.7 and known LLM variance; only planning runtimes are averaged over 5 runs. No variance, seeds, or confidence intervals are reported for the main claims, so the reported 24.5x API reduction and 'world model that captured the core mechanics' are not reliably supported.

The main baseline (GPT-o1 outputting action sequences from text states) is weak and somewhat of a strawman: it is not a model-based RL baseline, nor a strong LLM-modulo/LLM-with-tools planner, nor a plan-then-execute LLM baseline. Given that the paper positions itself as an alternative to deep RL and to model-based RL, the absence of any RL or neural world-model comparison is a significant gap.

The comparison against EMPA reuses numbers from Tsividis et al. (2021) with different step budgets and accounting, so it is unclear whether the head-to-head in Table 3 is apples-to-apples. Similarly, the WorldCoder comparison is inconsistent (stated as 'Minigrid environments used in their paper' then reported as 'Baby AI domain'), and only total tokens/success are given without seeds or detail on budget fairness.

The domains and level counts are small (5, 4, 17, 13 levels), and several results tables are internally confusing (e.g., Table 3 lists GPT-o1 'Steps Taken = 9' with 20% success; Table 4 level RTs vary by orders of magnitude). This makes it hard to assess the breadth of the generality claim.

Reproducibility is limited: the core PDDL files, Python predicate/checker functions, and the exact prompts/replay buffers are only partially shown in an appendix and not released. Since the PDDL abstractions are the crux of the method, their absence blocks independent verification.

The contribution is essentially an engineering composition of existing components (Fast Downward + BFS + LLM code synthesis), and the paper does not isolate which component drives the gains (e.g., is bilevel planning the cause, the PDDL goal specification, or the LLM's ability to write a good Python model?). The ablation focuses on planning time rather than on the source of sample-efficiency gains.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and well-motivated integration of LLM-based program synthesis with hierarchical PDDL/bilevel planning, extending theory-based RL beyond VGDL-style theories.
The architecture is clearly described, with an iterative loop of high-level planning, low-level BFS planning, execution, and LLM-based transition-model refinement guided by abstract subplan labels.

The experiments cover several challenging grid-world domains (Sokoban, Push Boulders, BabyAI, KekeCompetition/Baba Is You) and compare against GPT-o1, EMPA, and WorldCoder, with additional ablations for bilevel planning and a data-contamination check.

The reported results support the main claims within the evaluated domains: TheoryCoder achieves higher success rates, lower LLM API usage, and better planning efficiency than the LLM-only baseline, and solves tasks where EMPA struggled.
The paper includes useful failure-mode analysis and an honest limitations section, particularly regarding hand-engineered abstractions and world-model overgeneralization.
weaknesses: The high-level abstractions, predicates, PDDL domain/problem files, and checker functions are hand-designed per domain; only the low-level transition model is learned. This substantially reduces the generality and scalability claims, since much of the key domain knowledge is injected by the human designer rather than learned.

The central TBRL limitation of restrictive theory languages is only partially addressed: the low-level theory is now Python, but the high-level theory still requires manually specifying appropriate PDDL operators and predicates for each new domain.

The evaluation is limited to deterministic, relatively small grid-world games. There is little evidence that the approach scales to continuous, stochastic, 3D, or more naturalistic domains, and some bilevel planning runtimes remain very large (e.g., hundreds of seconds).

Statistical rigor is limited: success rates and API-call counts appear to be reported without repeated runs, confidence intervals, or error bars, despite the nondeterminism of LLM-based program synthesis and planning.

The main LLM-only baseline is a text-based planner without explicit symbolic abstractions, low-level transition model, or bilevel planner. TheoryCoder is given significant hand-designed high-level structure and domain descriptions, so the comparison does not fully isolate the contribution of low-level world-model learning.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: prompts are provided, but the domain-specific abstractions, natural-language domain descriptions, checker implementations, and code/data release status are unclear, which could make exact replication difficult.

The comparison with EMPA uses only a limited subset of games and different evaluation budgets/metrics, and the learning-efficiency metric may not fully capture environment sample efficiency versus LLM query efficiency.
